title: How Far to Trust a Prediction

steps.body: Predictions are most reliable **inside** the range of the data. Stretching far **beyond** it — called **extrapolation** — is risky: the trend may not continue. A line fit to weeks 1–6 may say little about week 50.

widget.prompt: A line is fit to data from x = 1 to x = 10. A prediction at x = 5 is likely more trustworthy than one at x = 40 because…

options.label: x = 5 is inside the measured range; x = 40 is far beyond it
options.feedback: Right — predictions inside the data range are more reliable.

options.label: x = 5 is a smaller number
options.feedback: Size isn't the point — x = 5 is INSIDE the data range, x = 40 is far outside it.

options.label: x = 40 is even
options.feedback: Even or odd is irrelevant — trust depends on staying inside the measured range.

options.label: both are equally reliable
options.feedback: They're not — x = 5 is inside the data, so its prediction is more reliable than x = 40's.

predict.prompt: A line was fit to data from x = 1 to 10. Does the line KNOW what happens beyond x = 10?

options.label: No — it just extends the pattern on faith
Beyond the data it's MORE accurate

predict.reveal: The line only ever saw x = 1 to 10 — past that it assumes the pattern continues, which the data never promised. Predictions inside the data deserve more trust.

steps.body: Data can also curve outside the range you measured. A plant grows steadily for weeks, then stops at full height — a straight line would keep predicting impossible growth. Real trends often bend once you leave the data.

explanationVariants: Predicting far beyond the measured data is extrapolation, and it can be unreliable.
Stretching the line well past the data is extrapolation.

widget.prompt: Using a line fit to ages 6–12 to predict a 40-year-old's height is an example of…

options.label: Extrapolation — predicting far beyond the data
options.feedback: Right — reaching far past the measured range is extrapolation, and it's risky.

options.label: A reliable prediction
options.feedback: Age 40 is far outside the 6–12 data — that's risky extrapolation, not reliable.

options.label: Finding the slope
options.feedback: This is about how far the prediction reaches, not computing slope — it's extrapolation.

options.label: Interpolation
options.feedback: Interpolation is predicting INSIDE the data — age 40 is far outside, so it's extrapolation.

widget.prompt: A line fit to a plant's first 6 weeks predicts it will be 3 meters tall at week 100. What's the problem?

options.label: The plant likely stops growing — the line can't be trusted that far out
options.feedback: Right — real growth levels off; the line over-predicts far beyond the data.

options.label: The slope was computed wrong
options.feedback: The math may be fine — the issue is trusting the line 94 weeks past the data.

options.label: Weeks can't be that large
options.feedback: Week 100 is a valid time — the problem is the trend won't stay linear that far out.

options.label: 3 meters is a round number
options.feedback: The value's roundness isn't the issue — it's extrapolating far beyond the data.

explanationVariants: A prediction at x = 8, inside data spanning x = 1 to 12, is the most trustworthy.
The prediction inside the data range (x = 8) is safest.

widget.prompt: A line is fit to data from x = 1 to x = 12. Which prediction is the most trustworthy?

options.label: x = 8
options.feedback: Right — x = 8 sits inside the measured range, so its prediction is most reliable.

options.label: x = 20
options.feedback: x = 20 is beyond the data (1–12) — less reliable than a prediction inside the range.

options.label: x = 100
options.feedback: x = 100 is far past the data — that's risky extrapolation.

options.label: x = 50
options.feedback: x = 50 is well outside the 1–12 range — a prediction inside it (like x = 8) is safer.

explanationVariants: Outside the measured data a real relationship can curve or level off, so a straight line may mislead.
Beyond the data, trends can change, so the line may not hold.

widget.prompt: Why can a line of best fit give a bad prediction far outside the data range?

options.label: The real trend may curve or level off out there
options.feedback: Right — beyond the data the relationship can change, so the line misleads.

options.label: Lines can't be extended
options.feedback: You CAN extend a line — the risk is that the real trend may not stay straight.

options.label: The slope becomes zero
options.feedback: The slope stays the same — the issue is the true trend may bend beyond the data.

options.label: Predictions are always wrong
options.feedback: Predictions inside the data are usually fine — it's far extrapolation that's risky.

explanationVariants: Inside the data range = reliable; far outside = risky extrapolation.
Sort by whether the x is inside the measured range or far beyond it.

widget.prompt: A line is fit to data from x = 2 to x = 15. Sort each prediction.

items.label: predict y at x = 90
items.feedback: x = 90 is far beyond 15 — risky extrapolation.

items.label: predict y at x = 200
items.feedback: x = 200 is far past the data — risky extrapolation.

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — inside the 2–15 range is reliable; far beyond it is risky extrapolation.
widget.successFeedback: All sorted — trust predictions inside the data, doubt far extrapolations.

hints: Check whether each x lands inside the data span 2–15.
Inside the range → reliable; far outside → risky.
x = 6 and x = 12 are inside; x = 90 and x = 200 are far beyond.

steps.body: Trust predictions inside the data range; far extrapolation is risky because trends can bend.
takeaways: Predictions inside the measured range are the most reliable.
Extrapolation — reaching far beyond the data — can mislead.
Real relationships may curve or level off outside the data.

concept.body: Predictions are most reliable inside the range of the data. Extrapolation — predicting far beyond the measured data — is risky because the real trend may curve or level off.

explanationVariants: A prediction inside the data range (x = 7 within 1–12) is the most trustworthy.
Inside the measured range is the reliable choice.

options.label: x = 7
options.feedback: Right — x = 7 is inside the data range, so it's most reliable.

options.label: x = 40
options.feedback: x = 40 is far beyond the data (1–12) — risky extrapolation.

options.label: x = 80
options.feedback: x = 80 is well outside the range — a prediction inside it is safer.

options.feedback: x = 500 is far past the data — that's risky extrapolation.
